CONTAMINATION_NEAR_MISS.fix: the probe now binds on the BOARD'S OWN canonical ids (ESPN_GAMEID 401857180-83) and asks whether those specific games are completed. They are all STATUS_SCHEDULED at 0-0. Identity-based, which is what the binding contract required in the first place.
CONTAMINATION_NEAR_MISS.severity: CAUGHT BEFORE PUBLICATION — no bad number reached a record
CONTAMINATION_NEAR_MISS.this_is_the_named_P0: RESULT_DATE_COHORT_CONTAMINATION — the same defect class as the 8/27 incident, arriving through a different door: not a matchup join without a date, but a date filter in the wrong timezone.
CONTAMINATION_NEAR_MISS.what_actually_saved_it: the guard was written to abort rather than to proceed on a surprising reading, so a wrong premise produced a halt instead of a grade. The lesson is not that the check was clever — it was wrong — but that a check which fails loudly gives you a chance to notice it is wrong. A silent version of the same query would have graded two 8/27 games as 8/28.
CONTAMINATION_NEAR_MISS.what_happened: the first version of the post-slate WNBA probe asked wehoop 'are there completed rows where date == 2026-08-28?'. It answered YES, 2 rows, and the module halted with ARCHIVE_STATE_CHANGED — telling me to go grade the cohort.
CONTAMINATION_NEAR_MISS.why_that_was_wrong: wehoop's `date` column is UTC. The two rows were ESPN 401857178 (GSV 79-60 NYL, 2026-08-28T00:00Z) and 401857179 (WSH 80-73 PHX, 2026-08-28T02:00Z) — both 8/27 EVENING ET games. Neither is on the 8/28 board. Both were already graded in the 8/27 review, where GSV 79-60 appears in finals_identified. A UTC date filter manufactures a two-game '8/28 result set' out of the previous slate.

FILING.R6_NOTE: this record was first written to the 8/27 review's path, overwriting it. That was an append-only violation: the 8/27 record would have been destroyed with no trace that it had ever said anything different. The 8/27 file was restored byte-for-byte from git and this review was filed at its own path. Disclosed rather than silently corrected.
FILING.naming_convention: night reviews are filed under the date they are WRITTEN, not the slate they review, because the review runs after midnight UTC. The 8/27 slate's review is therefore at data/audit/2026-08-28_end_of_night_review.json (record_id END-OF-NIGHT-REVIEW-2026-08-27). Read the record_id, not the filename, to know which slate a review covers.

LESSON_ON_THE_FLAGGING_HEURISTIC.action: carried into the 8/29 cycle as a required check — verify starter SIDES against an archive after the fact for every game, not only for rows that looked contentious.
LESSON_ON_THE_FLAGGING_HEURISTIC.consequence: the side-swap defect class is broader than the flagged set, and the flag was tracking SOURCE CONFLICT rather than SWAP RISK. Those are different things: the dangerous case is confident agreement on a reversed pair, which produces no conflict to notice.
LESSON_ON_THE_FLAGGING_HEURISTIC.what_happened: the three rows I flagged and chased all day resolved as immaterial (MIA@WSH), cleared (CWS@MIN) or already-correct (PIT@STL, COL@ATL). The row that actually carried an 11.75-point error was LAD@DET, which was never flagged at all.
LESSON_ON_THE_FLAGGING_HEURISTIC.why_it_slipped: the acquisition recorded 'starters consistent across 2 snippets' and treated agreement as clearance. Two sources agreeing can be wrong the same way, especially if they share an upstream. Agreement is not independence.
